subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage: Note for Mrs Rao at the art school. Usha came to me on Sunday and whispered that she wants art classes but is afraid to ask her parents, because they listen to me. I said I would mention it first, on Monday, over tea. I did: I said only that Usha has been drawing every day and might enjoy a class. Her mother said, "Let us hear from Usha." At dinner Usha spoke up about the colours she wants to learn with, the timings after school, and how she will keep her homework done. Her father asked about the fees, so we plan to visit your class on Saturday. Nani

qa.q: What did Nani say she would mention on Monday over tea?
qa.a: Nani would mention that Usha has been drawing every day and might enjoy a class.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she whispered to Nani on Sunday?
qa.a: Afraid of asking her parents directly, which is why she whispered and wanted Nani to speak first.

qa.q: What other approach could help Usha if her parents remain unsure?
qa.a: She could offer to try a few sessions or show them her drawings, because it gives them something to see before a bigger decision.

qa.q: How might Usha's mother have felt when Nani mentioned the idea?
qa.a: Open to it but wanting to hear from Usha herself, since she said "Let us hear from Usha", which suggests she cares what Usha wants. 🙂

grounding: A child asks her grandmother to raise the art-class idea first, then adds her own reasons at dinner.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage:
Tuesday
It worked, sort of. On Sunday I told Granny about the art classes at the community hall and asked if she could bring it up first, because when Granny says something, Mum and Dad actually stop and listen. Tonight at dinner Granny said, "That child draws on every scrap of paper in this house. Have you seen the art classes near the library?" Dad put down his fork. Then I said my part, the one I'd practised: the classes are on Saturdays, so no school is missed, my friend Yusuf's sister goes, and I'd give up TV on Saturday mornings. Mum said she'd call the hall tomorrow and ask about the fee. Granny winked at me across the table.
Elizabeth

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when Granny winked?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt hopeful and supported, pleased that the plan was working. 😊

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth do if the fee turns out to be a problem?
qa.a: Talk it over with Mum and Dad and ask the hall about other options, rather than giving up.

qa.q: How does Granny seem to experience her part?
qa.a: Granny enjoys it, winking across the table, glad to help.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child asking a grandparent to raise the idea of art classes first, then adding reasons at dinner.

subtype: Approach: asking a grandparent to speak first [Action]
passage: In their kasba near Amritsar, a retired drawing teacher had started art classes in the gurdwara hall on Sunday afternoons. Jaya wanted to go more than anything, but her father always called drawing "time-pass". So on Thursday, while Dadi was shelling peas in the courtyard, Jaya sat beside her. "Dadi, will you tell Papa about the classes first? He always listens to you." Dadi smiled. At dinner on Friday Dadi said, "Gurleen's mother says the drawing classes are good. Our Jaya's hands are always busy with a pencil." Papa grunted. Then Jaya spoke clearly: "It's only Sunday afternoons, after my homework. Gurleen is going too. And I'll help Dadi with the peas first." Papa looked at Dadi, then at Jaya. "Try it for a month."

qa.a: In the gurdwara hall on Sunday afternoons.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel about asking Papa directly?
qa.a: Nervous, since Papa always calls drawing 'time-pass'.

qa.q: What else could Jaya do if Papa had said no?
qa.a: Show him her drawings and ask what would change his mind, keeping Dadi on her side.
He grunts at first, then, after hearing both Dadi and Jaya, agrees to a month's trial.

grounding: A girl asks her grandmother to mention art classes first, since her father listens to her, and then adds her own reasons.
